The Hairy-crested antbird (Rhegmatorhina melanosticta) is a medium-sized obligate ant-following species inhabiting lowland terra firme forests of western Amazonia. Field studies indicate that incubating adults maintain a remarkably stable brood chamber temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a thermal regime under which a predictable sequence of early-life events unfolds. The embryonic period concludes with hatching at approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] of incubation when maintained at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], though this developmental rate appears slightly accelerated under the more typical nest temperature of 40.2 °C. Fledging, marked by the chick's first departure from the nest cavity, occurs 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a relatively short nestling phase consistent with the high predation pressure characteristic of understory avian communities. Neonates emerge with a wet weight at birth of 4.3 grams [Wwb = 4.3 grams], a modest initial mass that necessitates intensive biparental provisioning throughout the nestling period.

As chicks transition into the juvenile stage, they begin to forage alongside their parents while gradually acquiring the skills necessary for independent prey capture. The attainment of sexual maturity in this species is characterized by the onset of gonadal development, with puberty occurring 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid maturation is typical of thamnophilid antbirds and likely reflects selection pressures associated with high adult turnover in a competitive, territory-based social system. Adult females ultimately reach a maximum wet weight of 31 grams [Wwi = 31 grams], placing them near the upper end of the body size range reported for the genus Rhegmatorhina. The energetic demands of sustaining this adult body mass and maintaining reproductive readiness are considerable, and field metabolic measurements help quantify these costs under natural thermal conditions.

Respirometry trials conducted on wild-caught individuals during the non-breeding season have provided critical data on the species' energetic physiology. Under controlled conditions at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], within the typical thermal neutral zone for tropical suboscine passerines, the maximum basal metabolic rate was measured at 74.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 74.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with the resting oxygen consumption rates documented for other ant-following thamnophilids of comparable body mass and suggests a moderate metabolic intensity that balances thermoregulatory demands with the energetic costs of active foraging behind army ant swarms. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting birds during their inactive nocturnal period to minimize the confounding effects of activity and digestive metabolism.

Reproductive output in the Hairy-crested antbird follows a pattern typical of many tropical passerines, characterized by small clutch sizes distributed across a protracted breeding season. Females produce two eggs per nest [N_R_i = two eggs per nest] and, under favorable conditions, initiate approximately one new nesting attempt annually [F_R_i = approximately one new nesting attempt annually], a reproductive tempo constrained by the extended period of intense parental care required to fledge successful young. The first successful brood generally occurs at 511 days after hatching [tR = 511 days after hatching] under the stable thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] typical of their shaded understory microhabitat, reflecting the time required for territory acquisition, pair formation, and attainment of full breeding competence following gonadal maturation. This delayed first reproduction is a common life-history trait among obligate ant-following birds, where competition for high-quality foraging territories can be intense.

Longevity records from mark-recapture studies in southeastern Peru indicate that the Hairy-crested antbird can attain a remarkable maximum lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years] in individuals maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a surprisingly extended duration for a small insectivorous passerine that experiences high daily mortality risk from predation and accidental injury while attending swarms. This substantial lifespan, combined with relatively low annual reproductive output, aligns with a slow life-history strategy in which adults invest heavily in self-maintenance and persist through multiple breeding seasons. The thermal environment of the understory remains remarkably stable at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] throughout much of the day due to the buffering effects of the canopy, providing a consistent physiological backdrop against which all life-history events, from the initial incubation period through the final years of senescence, unfold with relatively little thermal perturbation.
